scenes.narration: Meet Nia. She's a site scout, and her new job sounds simple. An AI company wants to build a giant data center campus, and Nia has to find it a home. Her boss gives her one rule. Don't look for workers. Look for the plug. This place will drink as much power as a whole city, every hour of every day. A century ago, companies went hunting for oil. Now Nia is hunting for cheap electricity. So could cheap electricity become the new oil?

scenes.narration: To keep her company, the team gave Nia a scale model of the campus. They call it Cubby. Cubby is a building that turns electricity into answers, and into heat. Once it's built, it needs surprisingly few people. What it needs is power, huge amounts of it, all day and all night, for years.

Nia's boss texts her a checklist. Cheap power. Lots of it. Ready soon. Cool enough. Close enough to the customers. And a government that says yes. Nia looks at the list, then at Cubby. That's not a building site, she says. That's a treasure map.

And Cubby has a lot of siblings. The International Energy Agency projects that by the end of this decade, the world's data centers could use about as much electricity as all of Japan uses today. That's a whole new industrial country, appearing on the map, and it has to plug in somewhere.

We've seen a map redrawn like this before. In the twentieth century, oil decided where whole cities boomed, which ports got busy, and which countries got rich. Refineries rose beside the wells, and tankers carried the rest of the world's share. Nia wonders whether electricity is about to redraw that map.

Let me draw why the plug matters so much. Here's oil. It's easy to move. Pump it into a tanker, and it crosses an ocean. Now here's electricity. To move it far, you need giant power lines that take years to build, and you lose some along the way. Nobody ships a waterfall. So when the energy can't come to the factory, the factory goes to the energy.

scenes.narration: And this has happened before. Meet aluminum, the metal in your soda can. You can't just dig it up. You have to tear it out of its ore with a massive electric current. Making a single ton takes about as much electricity as an American home uses in more than a year. That's why people call aluminum solid electricity.

So the smelters went hunting for cheap power, exactly like Nia. In the nineteen sixties, Iceland built its first giant dam mainly to power its first aluminum smelter. Electricity in, metal out, ships to the world. Iceland's national power company still sells most of its power to heavy industry.

Or take Canada. It doesn't mine any of the ore aluminum comes from. Yet it's one of the world's big aluminum makers, with almost all of its smelters in Quebec, beside giant hydro dams. The ore sails in. The metal sails out. In a way, Quebec exports its rivers, one ingot at a time.

Now here's the twist. A data center is a smelter for the digital age. Electricity goes in. Answers come out. And answers are even easier to ship than metal. They travel down a fiber cable, almost at the speed of light. So Nia starts where the smelters went first.

scenes.narration: So Nia pins up a map of the cheapest, cleanest, biggest power on Earth, and books a lot of flights. Six pins. One suitcase. And one very excited scale model in the seat beside her.

First pin, northern Norway. Nearly all of Norway's electricity comes from falling water, and the far north has more of it than it can use. In the port town of Narvik, a new AI campus was announced as Stargate Norway, picked for hydropower and cool air. Since then, the tenant changed, and Microsoft became the big customer. The plug stayed the same. Norway's oil fortune is the story we told in Why Norway Is So Rich. This is its other energy.

Second pin, Iceland. Power from rivers and from the heat under the ground, and cold air that cools servers almost for free. Data centers came here years ago. But Nia hears a warning. When the reservoirs ran low, Iceland's big power company had to sell less power. Cheap doesn't mean endless.
Third pin, Quebec. Nia checks the price. Here, a giant factory pays less than a quarter of what the same factory would pay in Boston. Cubby is thrilled.

Then the catch. Hydro-Québec now says its days of surplus power are over. Big new users need the government's permission to plug in. And it has proposed a new rate just for data centers, more than double what big industry pays today. The cheapest plug in North America is starting to act like an oil producer. It wants a bigger share of the prize.

Fourth pin, Texas. Cheap natural gas, huge wind and solar farms, and a grid famous for plugging new customers in fast. In Abilene, the first giant Stargate halls switched on in twenty twenty-five. Now everyone wants in, so many that the grid operator is sorting through requests that dwarf everything Texas uses today. What all this means for household bills is the story of Why AI Could Make Your Electricity Bill Explode.

Fifth pin, the Gulf. Sunshine nearly every day, cheap gas, and money to spend. Saudi Arabia signed solar contracts at about a penny per kilowatt hour, among the cheapest ever. And Abu Dhabi is building an AI campus planned to grow to the size of several big power plants. The countries that sold the world oil now want to sell it computing.

But Nia sweats through the catch. The sun sets every evening, and a data center never sleeps, so the desert campuses still lean on gas at night. And cooling hot chips in desert heat burns extra power. Cheap sunshine is a head start, not a free ride.

Sixth pin, Brazil. Its electricity is mostly renewable, from rivers, wind and sun, and TikTok has confirmed a data center in Ceará, fed by new wind farms. But Nia finds a catch on the bill. Nearly half of what Brazil's power companies collect goes to taxes and charges. The power is cheap to make and expensive to buy. Brazil has just passed a special tax deal to win data centers anyway.

Let me draw what Nia actually learned. The price on the map is only the first block. Stack on top of it the wires to bring the power in, then the taxes and charges, then the cooling, then the distance to the people using the answers. And under all of it, the hardest one to see, the wait. A cheap power plant behind a full grid is like an oil field with no pipeline.

scenes.narration: And the wait can be the biggest cost of all. The IEA found that in parts of Europe, a data center can wait as long as a decade for a grid connection. Building the data center itself is much faster than that. Cubby can be ready long before the plug is.

Ireland shows what happens when the plugs win too fast. Data centers there now use more than a fifth of all the metered electricity in the country, more than all the homes in its cities. Around Dublin, the grid got so tight that new data centers now have to bring their own power.

Then there's heat and distance. Chips run hot, and cooling them takes water or even more power, which is why the cold north looks so good. But distance matters too. Training a giant AI model can happen far away. Answering your question happens best close to you. So the far north wins one kind of job, and the big cities keep another.

scenes.narration: And then, politics. When power is cheap, voters notice who gets it. Norway moved to block new crypto mines. Quebec decides who plugs in. Ireland makes newcomers bring their own power. Texas passed a law letting the grid tell giant users to cut back in an emergency. Cheap electricity, it turns out, is a resource governments guard, just like oil.

Let me draw the big difference. Oil made one world market. A barrel costs roughly the same wherever you buy it, plus shipping. So oil money flowed to whoever owned the wells. Electricity makes lots of little local markets, each one stuck behind its own wires. So the prize doesn't go to whoever has the most energy. It goes to whoever can deliver it fast, in huge blocks, and keep it on.

scenes.narration: So, could cheap electricity become the new oil? In one way, yes. Just like oil a century ago, it's deciding where the next giant industries land, and countries are already competing for them with dams, solar fields and tax deals. But in another way, no. Oil could be shipped to anyone. Electricity has to be used close to where it's made. So the new oil isn't just cheap power. It's cheap power you can plug into now, and that a country is willing to share.

So who's winning right now? The cold hydro north, for the giant training halls. Texas and the Gulf, for speed and scale. Quebec, if you can get its permission. Brazil, if it can make its power bill lighter. And the losers? Places with cheap power and a grid that can't take one more plug.

Nia files her report. Not one pin, but a pattern. The giant training halls go where power is cheap and cold air is free. The answering machines stay near the cities. And the winners are the places that build wires as fast as data centers. Cubby finally gets its plug. And Nia gets her next assignment. Find the plug for the robot factories.
